s.u1.title: The force that reaches everywhere
s.u1.blurb: Why an apple falls and the moon does not, and why those turn out to be the same question.
s.u2.title: Free fall
s.u2.blurb: Everything falls at the same rate, and it has nothing at all to do with how heavy it is.
s.u3.title: Mass and weight
s.u3.blurb: One of them is the same on the moon and the other is a sixth. Telling them apart is most of this topic.
s.u4.title: Thrust and pressure
s.u4.blurb: The same force spread over a different area. A nail and a camel's foot are the two ends of one idea.
s.u5.title: Why things float
s.u5.blurb: Water pushes up on anything put into it. Whether that is enough is a question about density.
s.u6.title: Archimedes
s.u6.blurb: How much does the water push up by? Exactly the weight of the water that is no longer there.
ch9.u1.newton:
Whirl a stone on a thread and it goes round in a circle. Its speed need not change, but its direction does at every point, so its velocity is changing and something must be pulling it. What pulls it is the thread, and it pulls towards the centre. A force that keeps a body on a circular path like this is called a centripetal force, which simply means centre-seeking. Let go and the stone leaves along the tangent, which is how you know the thread was doing the work.

The moon goes round the earth, so something must be pulling it towards the earth, and there is no thread.

Newton's step was to guess that the thing pulling the moon is the same thing that pulls an apple off a tree. Nobody had put those two together, because an apple falls and the moon plainly does not. His answer is that the moon is falling, all the time, and missing, because it is also moving sideways fast enough to keep going round.

If the earth pulls the apple, the apple pulls the earth back just as hard, by the third law. We never see the earth move because its mass is so enormous that the same force gives it no acceleration worth measuring.
a.ch9-u1-read-1.title: The apple and the moon
ch9.u1.law:
Every object in the universe attracts every other object. The force between two of them is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres.

F = G Mm / d²

G is the universal gravitational constant, 6.673 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg², measured by Henry Cavendish with a very sensitive balance over a century after Newton wrote the law down. Its unit comes straight out of rearranging the equation.

Two things about that formula are worth sitting with.

The first is how small G is. There is a gravitational force between you and the person sitting next to you, and it is far too small to notice. Gravitation only becomes important when at least one of the masses is enormous.

The second is the square on the bottom. Double the distance and the force does not halve: it falls to a quarter. Make the distance six times bigger and the force is one thirty-sixth of what it was.

The word universal is doing real work. The same law, with the same G, governs a falling apple, the moon in its orbit, the planets round the Sun and the tides.
a.ch9-u1-read-2.title: The universal law
ch9.u1.sort.i0.label: One of the two masses is doubled
ch9.u1.sort.i0.why: F is proportional to each mass, so doubling one doubles F.
ch9.u1.sort.i1.label: The distance between them is doubled
ch9.u1.sort.i1.why: The distance is squared on the bottom, so F falls to a quarter, not a half.
ch9.u1.sort.i2.label: The distance is halved
ch9.u1.sort.i2.why: Half the distance means a quarter on the bottom, so F becomes four times bigger.
ch9.u1.sort.i3.label: Both masses are doubled and the distance is doubled too
ch9.u1.sort.i3.why: The top goes up four times and the bottom goes up four times. They cancel exactly.
ch9.u1.sort.i4.label: The distance is made three times larger
ch9.u1.sort.i4.why: Three squared is nine, so F drops to a ninth.
ch9.u1.sort.i5.label: Both objects are carried to the moon, keeping the same separation
ch9.u1.sort.i5.why: G is universal and neither mass nor the distance has changed. Where the pair happens to be makes no difference at all.
a.ch9-u1-sort-3.title: What happens to the force?
a.ch9-u1-sort-3.blurb: Every one of these is read straight off F = GMm over d squared. The square is what catches people.
ch9.u1.calc.c0.prompt: The force of gravitation between two objects is 36 N. The distance between them is then made six times larger, with nothing else changed. What is the force now?
ch9.u1.calc.c0.g0: F = 36 N at the original distance
ch9.u1.calc.c0.s0: F is inversely proportional to the square of the distance
ch9.u1.calc.c0.s1: Six squared is 36, so F becomes 36 times smaller
ch9.u1.calc.c0.trap: Dividing by 6 to get 6 N. The square is the whole content of the inverse-square law.
ch9.u1.calc.c1.prompt: What is the force of gravitation between the earth and a 1 kg object resting on its surface? Take the mass of the earth as 6 × 10²⁴ kg, its radius as 6.4 × 10⁶ m, and G as 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg².
ch9.u1.calc.c1.s1: The bottom is (6.4 × 10⁶) squared, which is about 4.1 × 10¹³
ch9.u1.calc.c1.s2: The top is 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹ times 6 × 10²⁴ times 1, which is 4.02 × 10¹⁴
ch9.u1.calc.c1.trap: Using the diameter instead of the radius. The distance in the law is to the centre of the earth, and you are standing one radius from it.
ch9.u1.calc.c2.prompt: Two 1 kg masses sit 1 m apart. What is the gravitational force between them? Take G as 6.7 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg², and give the answer as a multiple of 10⁻¹¹ N.
ch9.u1.calc.c2.trap: Expecting a number you could feel. This is why nobody notices the pull of the person sitting next to them.
ask.ch9-u1-calc-4.whyweak.q: If gravitation is so weak, why does it run the solar system?
ask.ch9-u1-calc-4.whyweak.a:
Because it is the only one of the four forces that never cancels.

Electric forces are enormously stronger, but matter contains equal amounts of positive and negative charge, so over any large object they almost exactly cancel out. Nothing cancels gravitation: there is no negative mass, so every kilogram adds to the pull and none of it subtracts.

So the weakest force wins at large scales by simply accumulating. The earth's pull on you is the sum of the pull of every kilogram in it, and that is six thousand billion billion tonnes of adding up.
a.ch9-u1-calc-4.title: Using the law
ch9.u1.quiz.q0.prompt: The distance between two objects is halved. What happens to the gravitational force between them?
ch9.u1.quiz.q0.f0: Right. The distance is squared, so halving it quarters the bottom of the fraction.
ch9.u1.quiz.q0.f1: That would be true if the distance were not squared. It is.
ch9.u1.quiz.q0.f2: The force goes up when the distance comes down, not the other way about.
ch9.u1.quiz.q1.prompt: Does an apple attract the earth?
ch9.u1.quiz.q1.o0: Yes, with exactly the same force the earth attracts it
ch9.u1.quiz.q1.f0: Right. It is a third law pair, so the two forces are equal.
ch9.u1.quiz.q1.o1: No, only the earth does the attracting
ch9.u1.quiz.q1.f1: Every object attracts every other object. That is what universal means.
ch9.u1.quiz.q1.o2: Yes, but with a much smaller force
ch9.u1.quiz.q1.f2: The forces are equal. What differs is the acceleration, because the masses do.
ch9.u1.quiz.q2.prompt: Why does the earth not visibly move towards a falling apple?
ch9.u1.quiz.q2.o0: Its mass is so large that the same force gives it no measurable acceleration
ch9.u1.quiz.q2.f0: Right. a = F/m, and the m here is six thousand billion billion tonnes.
ch9.u1.quiz.q2.o1: The apple's pull on the earth is far too small to exist
ch9.u1.quiz.q2.f1: It exists and is equal to the earth's pull on the apple. It is the acceleration that is tiny.
ch9.u1.quiz.q2.o2: The earth is fixed in space
ch9.u1.quiz.q2.f2: The earth moves a great deal. It is not anchored to anything.
a.ch9-u1-quiz-5.title: The universal law
ch9.u2.lab.predict.prompt: You drop a 1 kg stone and then a 5 kg stone from the same height, with no air in the way. What happens to the acceleration?
ch9.u2.lab.predict.o0: The 5 kg stone accelerates five times as fast
ch9.u2.lab.predict.o1: The 5 kg stone accelerates a little faster
ch9.u2.lab.predict.o2: Both accelerate at exactly the same rate
ch9.u2.lab.observe: Run the three tasks and keep your eye on the acceleration figure above the graphs.
ch9.u2.lab.explain:
The acceleration stays at 9.8 m/s² whatever you do to the mass, and the two graphs come out identical.

The reason is in the algebra. The earth pulls harder on a heavier object, so F goes up with m. But the acceleration is F divided by m, and the m cancels. A heavier object has more pull on it and exactly as much more to move.

This is why Galileo is said to have dropped two different weights from the Leaning Tower, and why a feather and a hammer fall together on the moon, where there is no air.
ch9.u2.lab.t1.label: Drop a 1 kg stone.
ch9.u2.lab.t1.asks: Note the acceleration. Write the number down before changing anything.
ch9.u2.lab.t2.label: Drop a 5 kg stone.
ch9.u2.lab.t2.asks: Same height, five times the mass. What is the acceleration now?
ch9.u2.lab.t3.label: Drop a half-kilogram stone.
ch9.u2.lab.t3.asks: Lighter than either. Has the acceleration moved at all?
ch9.u2.lab.closing: g does not depend on the mass of the falling object. A bigger mass has a bigger pull on it and exactly as much more to shift, and the two cancel.
a.ch9-u2-lab-1.title: Drop a heavy one and a light one
a.ch9-u2-lab-1.blurb: The same drop with the mass slider moved. Watch the acceleration readout, not the ball.
ch9.u2.paper.predict.prompt: You drop a flat sheet of paper and a stone from the same height at the same instant. Then you crumple the same sheet into a tight ball and drop it against the stone again. What changes?
ch9.u2.paper.predict.o0: Nothing. The paper weighs the same either way
ch9.u2.paper.predict.o1: The crumpled paper lands much closer to the stone
ch9.u2.paper.predict.o2: The crumpled paper now lands after the flat sheet
ch9.u2.paper.predict.o3: The stone lands later the second time
ch9.u2.paper.observe: Drop from as high as you safely can, and have someone at floor level watching for which lands first.
ch9.u2.paper.explain:
Crumpling does not change the paper's mass by a milligram. What it changes is the area the air has to push on.

Air resistance is what made the flat sheet fall slowly, not its lightness. Reduce the area and the resistance drops, and the paper falls almost as fast as the stone. In a jar with the air pumped out they land together exactly.
ch9.u2.do.steps:
1. Hold a flat sheet of paper in one hand and a stone in the other, at the same height.
2. Release both at the same instant. Have a partner below call which landed first.
3. Repeat twice to be sure.
4. Now crumple a second, identical sheet into a tight ball.
5. Drop the ball against the stone and call the result again.
6. Record the mass of the paper before and after crumpling, if a balance is available.
ch9.u2.do.watch: Someone will say the crumpled paper became heavier. Weigh it if you can: the mass is identical, and that is the whole experiment.
ask.ch9-u2-do-2.vacuum.q: Would they really land together with no air at all?
ask.ch9-u2-do-2.vacuum.a:
Yes, exactly together, and this has been filmed.

On the Apollo 15 mission an astronaut dropped a hammer and a falcon feather on the moon, where there is no atmosphere. They hit the ground at the same instant.

It also works in a glass jar with the air pumped out, which is how the demonstration is usually done in a laboratory. A coin and a feather, released together, fall together.
a.ch9-u2-do-2.title: A sheet of paper and a stone
a.ch9-u2-do-2.blurb: They do not land together. Crumple the paper and they nearly do, which tells you what was in the way.
ch9.u2.g:
Put the universal law next to the second law and g falls out.

The pull on an object of mass m at the surface is F = G M m / R², where M is the mass of the earth and R its radius. The second law says that same force is F = mg. Set the two equal and the m cancels from both sides:

g = G M / R²

Put the numbers in, with M = 6 × 10²⁴ kg and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, and g comes to 9.8 m/s².

Notice what is missing from that equation: the mass of the falling object. It cancelled, and that cancellation is why everything falls at the same rate.

g is not quite constant. The earth is slightly flattened, so R is smaller at the poles and g is a little larger there than at the equator. It also falls off with height. For anything happening near the ground, 9.8 m/s² is close enough, and many problems use 10 to keep the arithmetic out of the way.

Because g is a constant acceleration, the three equations of motion work unchanged with a replaced by g: v = u + gt, s = ut + ½gt², and v² = u² + 2gs. Take g as positive when the object is going down and negative when it is going up.
a.ch9-u2-read-3.title: Where 9.8 comes from
ch9.u2.calc.c0.prompt: A stone is dropped from rest and falls for 3 s. How fast is it moving? Take g as 10 m/s².
ch9.u2.calc.c0.trap: Answering 45, which is how far it fell, not how fast it is going.
ch9.u2.calc.c1.prompt: The same stone. How far has it fallen in those 3 s?
ch9.u2.calc.c1.s0: Use s = ut + half g t squared
ch9.u2.calc.c1.s1: The first term is zero because u is zero
ch9.u2.calc.c1.trap: Multiplying 30 m/s by 3 s to get 90. The speed climbed from zero, so the average was 15, not 30.
ch9.u2.calc.c2.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up at 20 m/s. How high does it rise? Take g as 10 m/s².
ch9.u2.calc.c2.g2: g = minus 10 m/s², because it opposes the motion
ch9.u2.calc.c2.trap: Forgetting that g is negative here. Going up, gravity is working against the motion.
ch9.u2.calc.c3.prompt: A stone is released from the top of a tower and hits the ground at 19.6 m/s. How tall is the tower? Take g as 9.8 m/s².
ch9.u2.calc.c3.trap: A coincidence worth noticing and not trusting: the height and the final speed come out as the same number here, and they will not next time.
a.ch9-u2-calc-4.title: Things falling and things thrown
ch9.u2.quiz.q0.prompt: Two stones, one 1 kg and one 10 kg, are dropped together with no air in the way. Which lands first?
ch9.u2.quiz.q0.f0: Right. The extra pull on the heavier one is exactly cancelled by its extra mass.
ch9.u2.quiz.q0.f1: It has ten times the pull on it and ten times as much to move. a = F/m is unchanged.
ch9.u2.quiz.q0.f2: Nothing gives the lighter one an advantage either.
ch9.u2.quiz.q1.prompt: Why does a flat sheet of paper fall more slowly than a stone?
ch9.u2.quiz.q1.o0: Air resistance, which acts on its large area
ch9.u2.quiz.q1.f0: Right, and crumpling the same sheet proves it: same mass, much less area, much faster fall.
ch9.u2.quiz.q1.f1: Lightness is not the reason. Crumple it and it falls fast while weighing exactly the same.
ch9.u2.quiz.q1.o2: Because paper is not attracted by gravity
ch9.u2.quiz.q1.f2: Everything with mass is attracted. Paper is not an exception.
ch9.u2.quiz.q2.prompt: What is the acceleration due to gravity at the surface of the earth?
ch9.u2.quiz.q2.f0: Right, and its value comes from g = GM over R squared.
ch9.u2.quiz.q2.f1: That is a speed, not an acceleration. The unit has a second squared in it.
ch9.u2.quiz.q2.f2: Newtons measure force. g is an acceleration.
a.ch9-u2-quiz-5.title: Free fall
ch9.u3.massweight:
In everyday speech, how much you weigh and how much mass you have are the same remark. In physics they are two different quantities with different units, and the difference shows up the moment you leave the earth.

Mass is the amount of matter in an object, and the measure of its inertia. It is the same number on the earth, on the moon and in deep space. Its unit is the kilogram.

Weight is the force with which the earth attracts an object. It is a force, so its unit is the newton, and it points downwards.

W = mg

Because g changes from place to place, weight changes from place to place. The moon's mass is much smaller than the earth's, so g on the moon is about a sixth of g here, and so is your weight. Your mass has not moved.

The weighing machine in a shop reads kilograms, which is why nobody notices any of this. It is measuring your weight with a spring and dividing by the g it was built for. Take it to the moon and it would read a sixth of the truth.
a.ch9-u3-read-1.title: Two words people use for one thing
ch9.u3.sort.i0.label: Measured in kilograms
ch9.u3.sort.i0.why: The kilogram is the SI unit of mass and of nothing else.
ch9.u3.sort.i1.label: Measured in newtons
ch9.u3.sort.i1.why: It is a force, and forces are measured in newtons.
ch9.u3.sort.i2.label: The same on the earth and on the moon
ch9.u3.sort.i2.why: Nothing about moving an object changes how much matter is in it.
ch9.u3.sort.i3.label: About a sixth as much on the moon
ch9.u3.sort.i3.why: Because g on the moon is about a sixth of g here, and W = mg.
ch9.u3.sort.i4.label: Has a direction: straight down
ch9.u3.sort.i4.why: A force always has one. Mass has none.
ch9.u3.sort.i5.label: A beam balance, with known weights in the other pan, reads this
ch9.u3.sort.i5.why: Both pans are in the same gravity, so whatever g happens to be cancels out. The same balance works on the moon.
ch9.u3.sort.i6.label: A spring balance hanging from a hook reads this
ch9.u3.sort.i6.why: The spring stretches by the pull on it, and that pull is the weight.
a.ch9-u3-sort-2.title: Which one does this describe?
ch9.u3.calc.c0.prompt: An object has a mass of 10 kg. What is its weight on the earth? Take g as 9.8 m/s².
ch9.u3.calc.c0.trap: Answering 10 N. Mass and weight are different quantities with different units.
ch9.u3.calc.c1.prompt: An object weighs 10 N on the earth. What does it weigh on the moon?
ch9.u3.calc.c1.g1: Weight on the moon is about a sixth of the weight on the earth
ch9.u3.calc.c1.trap: Answering 60 N. The moon's gravity is weaker, so the weight goes down, not up.
ch9.u3.calc.c2.prompt: A 10 kg object is carried to the moon. What is its mass there?
ch9.u3.calc.c2.s0: Mass does not depend on where the object is
ch9.u3.calc.c2.s1: So it is the same number
ch9.u3.calc.c2.trap: Dividing by six. That is what happens to the weight, and the mass is untouched.
ch9.u3.calc.c3.prompt: A bag of gold gives the same reading on a spring balance at the equator and at the North Pole. Where is there more gold in the bag? Answer with one word, equator or pole.
ch9.u3.calc.c3.g0: Equal readings on a spring balance, so equal weights
ch9.u3.calc.c3.g1: g is larger at the poles than at the equator
ch9.u3.calc.c3.s0: W = mg, so m = W over g
ch9.u3.calc.c3.s1: The same W with a larger g underneath gives a smaller m
ch9.u3.calc.c3.s2: So the pole bag holds less gold
ch9.u3.calc.c3.trap: Trusting a spring balance to compare amounts of gold between two places. Only a beam balance does that honestly.
ask.ch9-u3-calc-3.weightless.q: Astronauts float in a space station. Have they lost their weight?
ask.ch9-u3-calc-3.weightless.a:
Almost none of it. At that height the earth's pull is still about nine tenths of what it is at the ground.

They float because the station and everything in it are falling, continuously, all the way round the earth. There is nothing underneath pushing back, so nothing feels heavy. You get a weaker version of it for a fraction of a second in a lift that starts downwards suddenly.

So the word weightless is a poor one. It is the force from the floor that has gone, not the pull from the earth.
a.ch9-u3-calc-3.title: Weight here and weight there
ch9.u3.quiz.q0.prompt: What is the SI unit of weight?
ch9.u3.quiz.q0.f0: Right. Weight is a force, and forces are measured in newtons.
ch9.u3.quiz.q0.f1: That is the unit of mass.
ch9.u3.quiz.q0.f2: That is the unit of pressure.
ch9.u3.quiz.q1.prompt: You travel to the moon. What happens to your mass and your weight?
ch9.u3.quiz.q1.o0: Mass stays the same, weight falls to about a sixth
ch9.u3.quiz.q1.f0: Right. W = mg, and it is g that changed.
ch9.u3.quiz.q1.o1: Both fall to about a sixth
ch9.u3.quiz.q1.f1: Mass does not depend on where you are. Only the weight does.
ch9.u3.quiz.q1.o2: Mass falls to about a sixth, weight stays the same
ch9.u3.quiz.q1.f2: That is the two swapped round.
ch9.u3.quiz.q2.prompt: A beam balance and a spring balance are both taken to the moon. Which still gives the right answer?
ch9.u3.quiz.q2.o0: The beam balance, because the same g acts on both pans
ch9.u3.quiz.q2.f0: Right. It compares two weights in the same gravity, so g cancels and the mass comes out right.
ch9.u3.quiz.q2.o1: The spring balance, because springs are not affected by gravity
ch9.u3.quiz.q2.f1: A spring balance measures the pull on the object, and on the moon that pull is a sixth.
ch9.u3.quiz.q2.o2: Neither works away from the earth
ch9.u3.quiz.q2.f2: Both work. Only one of them still means what it did on the earth.
a.ch9-u3-quiz-4.title: Mass and weight
ch9.u4.pressure:
Press a drawing pin into a board with your thumb. The same force passes through the flat head and out of the sharp tip, and the tip goes into the wood while the head does nothing to your thumb.

The force acting on a surface at right angles to it is called thrust. What changed between the head and the tip is not the thrust. It is the area the thrust was spread over.

Pressure = thrust / area

The unit is the newton per square metre, which is given its own name, the pascal, after Blaise Pascal.

Once you have that, a lot of design falls into place. A knife is sharpened to make the area small and the pressure large. A camel's foot is broad to make the area large and the pressure small, which is why it does not sink into sand. A tank weighs tonnes and rests on wide continuous tracks for the same reason. Buildings are given wide foundations so the ground underneath is not asked to carry too much on any one patch.

Stand on loose sand and your feet sink. Lie down on the same sand and you do not, with exactly the same weight.
a.ch9-u4-read-1.title: The same force, spread differently
ch9.u4.calc.c0.prompt: A wooden block of mass 5 kg measures 40 cm by 20 cm by 10 cm. What thrust does it exert on a table? Take g as 9.8 m/s².
ch9.u4.calc.c0.s0: The thrust is the weight of the block
ch9.u4.calc.c0.trap: Trying to use the dimensions. The thrust is the same whichever face is down.
ch9.u4.calc.c1.prompt: The same block stands on its 20 cm by 10 cm face. What pressure does it exert?
ch9.u4.calc.c1.s0: Convert to metres: 0.2 m by 0.1 m, which is 0.02 m²
ch9.u4.calc.c1.s1: Pressure = thrust over area, so 49 divided by 0.02
ch9.u4.calc.c1.trap: Leaving the area in square centimetres. 200 cm² is 0.02 m², not 200 m² and not 2 m².
ch9.u4.calc.c2.prompt: The same block now lies on its 40 cm by 20 cm face. What pressure does it exert?
ch9.u4.calc.c2.g1: Area = 0.4 m by 0.2 m, which is 0.08 m²
ch9.u4.calc.c2.trap: Expecting the thrust to change too. The block weighs the same on any face; only the spread differs.
ask.ch9-u4-calc-2.whysame.q: Why does the thrust stay at 49 N on every face?
ask.ch9-u4-calc-2.whysame.a:
Because the thrust here is the weight of the block, and nothing about turning it over changes its mass.

The block presses down with 49 N whichever way up it is. All that changes is how many square metres of table are sharing that 49 N, and that is what pressure measures.

It is a useful check in any problem of this kind: if your thrust changed between two parts of the same question, something has gone wrong.
a.ch9-u4-calc-2.title: One block, two faces
ch9.u4.sort.bin.0: Made small on purpose, for high pressure
ch9.u4.sort.bin.1: Made large on purpose, for low pressure
ch9.u4.sort.i0.label: The tip of a nail
ch9.u4.sort.i0.why: A tiny area turns an ordinary hammer blow into enough pressure to part the wood.
ch9.u4.sort.i1.label: The foot of a camel
ch9.u4.sort.i1.why: A broad soft foot spreads the weight so it does not sink into sand.
ch9.u4.sort.i2.label: The edge of a knife
ch9.u4.sort.i2.why: Sharpening is the business of reducing the area the force has to work through.
ch9.u4.sort.i3.label: The tracks of an army tank
ch9.u4.sort.i3.why: More than a thousand tonnes on a continuous belt, so the ground under any patch carries very little.
ch9.u4.sort.i4.label: The foundations of a building
ch9.u4.sort.i4.why: Wide footings so no part of the soil is asked to carry more than it can.
ch9.u4.sort.i5.label: The strap of a school bag
ch9.u4.sort.i5.why: A broad strap spreads the same load across more of your shoulder, which is why a thin string hurts.
a.ch9-u4-sort-3.title: Made sharp, or made wide?
a.ch9-u4-sort-3.blurb: Every one of these is a decision about area, taken for a reason.
ch9.u4.quiz.q0.f0: Right, and its unit is the pascal, which is one newton per square metre.
ch9.u4.quiz.q0.f1: Multiplying would make a wide foot press harder, which is the opposite of what happens.
ch9.u4.quiz.q0.f2: That is the thrust in these problems, before the area is taken into account.
ch9.u4.quiz.q1.prompt: Why is it harder to carry a school bag with a thin strap than with a broad one?
ch9.u4.quiz.q1.o0: The same load is spread over a smaller area, so the pressure is higher
ch9.u4.quiz.q1.f0: Right. The bag's weight has not changed. Only the area taking it has.
ch9.u4.quiz.q1.o1: A thin strap makes the bag heavier
ch9.u4.quiz.q1.f1: The weight of the bag is the same whichever strap it has.
ch9.u4.quiz.q1.o2: A thin strap pulls downwards harder
ch9.u4.quiz.q1.f2: The pull is the weight, and that has not changed either.
ch9.u4.quiz.q2.prompt: A block is turned from its small face onto its large face. What happens?
ch9.u4.quiz.q2.o0: The thrust stays the same and the pressure falls
ch9.u4.quiz.q2.f0: Right. The thrust is the weight, which has not changed. The area has.
ch9.u4.quiz.q2.o1: Both the thrust and the pressure fall
ch9.u4.quiz.q2.f1: The block weighs the same on any face, so the thrust cannot fall.
ch9.u4.quiz.q2.o2: The thrust falls and the pressure stays the same
ch9.u4.quiz.q2.f2: The pressure is exactly the thing that changed.
a.ch9-u4-quiz-4.title: Thrust and pressure
ch9.u5.bottle.predict.prompt: You push a sealed empty bottle down into a bucket of water. What happens to the upward push you can feel as it goes deeper?
ch9.u5.bottle.predict.o0: It stays the same all the way down
ch9.u5.bottle.predict.o1: It grows until the bottle is fully under, then stops growing
ch9.u5.bottle.predict.o2: It grows all the way to the bottom of the bucket
ch9.u5.bottle.predict.o3: It disappears once the bottle is under
ch9.u5.bottle.observe: Push slowly and notice the exact moment the push stops getting harder.
ch9.u5.bottle.explain:
The upward push grows while more and more of the bottle is under the water, and stops growing the moment the bottle is completely submerged. Push it deeper still and nothing more happens.

That tells you what the push depends on: how much water the bottle is taking the place of. Once it is fully under, it is displacing its own volume and cannot displace any more.

Release it and it comes straight back up, because the upward push is larger than its weight.
ch9.u5.do.steps:
1. Stopper the empty bottle tightly and float it in a bucket of water.
2. Push it down slowly with one hand and notice how the push changes as more of it goes under.
3. Find the point where pushing deeper no longer feels any harder, and note where the water line is on the bottle.
4. Let go and watch what it does.
5. If you have a second bottle with some sand in it, repeat and compare.
ch9.u5.do.watch: A student who says the push keeps growing all the way to the bottom. Have them stop and feel for the moment it levels off, which is when the bottle is just covered.
a.ch9-u5-do-1.title: Push a bottle under water
a.ch9-u5-do-1.blurb: An empty stoppered bottle and a bucket. The push you feel is the whole topic.
ch9.u5.density:
Every object put into a fluid is pushed upwards. That upward force is called buoyancy, or upthrust. Both the water in a bucket and the air in this room do it.

Whether an object floats or sinks is a contest between two forces: its weight pulling it down, and the upthrust pushing it up.

The useful way to settle that contest is density, which is mass per unit volume. An iron nail is denser than water, so the water it displaces weighs less than the nail does, the upthrust loses, and the nail sinks. A piece of cork of the same mass is far less dense, so it floats.

An object less dense than the liquid floats on it. An object more dense sinks.

This is why a solid sheet of iron sinks and a ship made of thousands of tonnes of it does not. The ship is mostly air. Counting the air inside the hull, its density is well below that of water, and the sea holds it up.
a.ch9-u5-read-2.title: Density decides it
ch9.u5.draw.caption: A block floating in water, with its weight and the upthrust marked. When it floats, the two are equal.
ch9.u5.draw.beaker.label: The beaker and the water
ch9.u5.draw.beaker.do: Draw a tall open container. Rule a horizontal line across it for the water surface, about two thirds of the way up.
ch9.u5.draw.beaker.does: The surface line matters more than it looks. Everything below it is pushing up on whatever is put in; everything above it is not.
ch9.u5.draw.block.label: The block, sitting low in the water
ch9.u5.draw.block.do: Draw a rectangle across the surface line, with most of it below the line and a little of it above. That is a block that floats.
ch9.u5.draw.block.does: How much of it sits below the line is not a free choice. It settles at the depth where the water it has pushed aside weighs exactly what the block weighs.
ch9.u5.draw.weight.label: The weight, pulling down
ch9.u5.draw.weight.do: From the middle of the block draw an arrow pointing straight down. Label it W. This is the earth pulling on the block, and it is mg.
ch9.u5.draw.weight.does: The weight acts whether the block is in water, in air or in space. Nothing about floating switches it off.
ch9.u5.draw.upthrust.label: The upthrust, pushing up
ch9.u5.draw.upthrust.do: From the same point draw an arrow of exactly the same length pointing straight up, out through the top of the block. Label it U.
ch9.u5.draw.upthrust.does: The water pushes up on everything put into it. The block floats because these two arrows are the same length, and it would sink if the upward one were shorter.
ch9.u5.draw.upthrust.p0: The upthrust equals the weight of the water the block has pushed aside. That is Archimedes' principle.
ch9.u5.draw.upthrust.p1: A floating object has pushed aside exactly its own weight of water, no more and no less.
ch9.u5.draw.upthrust.p2: Push it further under and it displaces more, the upthrust grows larger than the weight, and it springs back up.
ch9.u5.draw.upthrust.p3: An object denser than water cannot displace its own weight even when fully under, so the arrows never match and it sinks.
ask.ch9-u5-draw-3.iron.q: If iron sinks, how does a ship made of iron float?
ask.ch9-u5-draw-3.iron.a:
Because a ship is mostly air, and density is about the whole object rather than what it is made of.

Take the same iron and roll it into a solid sheet and it sinks at once: that sheet is about eight times as dense as water. Build it into a hull with a huge empty space inside and the mass is unchanged while the volume is enormous. Divide one by the other and the average density of the ship comes out below that of water.

Which is why a hull with a hole in it sinks. Water comes in, takes the place of the air, and the average density climbs past that of water.
a.ch9-u5-draw-3.title: Draw the two forces on a floating block
a.ch9-u5-draw-3.blurb: A block floating in a beaker, and the two arrows that explain why it stays there.
ch9.u5.calc.c0.prompt: A substance has a mass of 50 g and a volume of 20 cm³. What is its density in g/cm³?
ch9.u5.calc.c0.s0: Density is mass divided by volume
ch9.u5.calc.c0.trap: Dividing the volume by the mass. Density is how much mass sits in each unit of volume.
ch9.u5.calc.c1.prompt: Water has a density of 1 g/cm³. Will that substance float or sink? Answer with one word.
ch9.u5.calc.c1.trap: Thinking a small object must float. Size has nothing to do with it; only the comparison of densities does.
ch9.u5.calc.c2.prompt: A sealed packet has a mass of 500 g and a volume of 350 cm³. Will it float or sink in water? Answer with one word.
ch9.u5.calc.c2.s0: Density is 500 divided by 350, which is about 1.43 g/cm³
ch9.u5.calc.c2.trap: Comparing the mass with the volume as plain numbers. It is the ratio that decides, not which number is bigger.
a.ch9-u5-calc-4.title: Will it float?
ch9.u5.quiz.q0.prompt: What decides whether an object floats in a liquid?
ch9.u5.quiz.q0.o0: Whether it is less dense than the liquid
ch9.u5.quiz.q0.f0: Right. Less dense floats, more dense sinks, whatever the size.
ch9.u5.quiz.q0.o1: Whether it is lighter than the liquid
ch9.u5.quiz.q0.f1: A ship is far heavier than a coin and the ship floats. Density is the comparison, not mass.
ch9.u5.quiz.q0.o2: Whether it is smaller than the container
ch9.u5.quiz.q0.f2: A pin is tiny and sinks. Size is not the test.
ch9.u5.quiz.q1.prompt: In which direction does the buoyant force on an immersed object act?
ch9.u5.quiz.q1.f0: Right, which is why it opposes the weight.
ch9.u5.quiz.q1.f1: That is the weight. The upthrust works against it.
ch9.u5.quiz.q1.o2: Along the direction the object is moving
ch9.u5.quiz.q1.f2: It is upwards whether the object is moving or still.
ch9.u5.quiz.q2.prompt: A block of plastic is released deep under water and rises. Why?
ch9.u5.quiz.q2.o0: The upthrust on it is larger than its weight
ch9.u5.quiz.q2.f0: Right. The two forces are unbalanced and the larger one is upwards.
ch9.u5.quiz.q2.o1: Water has no weight of its own to hold it down
ch9.u5.quiz.q2.f1: Water is heavy, and that weight is where the upthrust comes from.
ch9.u5.quiz.q2.o2: Gravity does not act under water
ch9.u5.quiz.q2.f2: Gravity acts everywhere. The block has a weight the whole way up.
a.ch9-u5-quiz-5.title: Floating and sinking
ch9.u6.stone.predict.prompt: A stone hangs from a spring balance and reads 5 N. You lower it slowly into a beaker of water. What does the reading do?
ch9.u6.stone.predict.o1: It falls as the stone goes in, and keeps falling once it is covered
ch9.u6.stone.predict.o2: It falls as the stone goes in, then stops falling once it is covered
ch9.u6.stone.predict.o3: It rises as the stone goes in
ch9.u6.stone.observe: Lower it a centimetre at a time and read the balance at each step.
ch9.u6.stone.explain:
The reading falls while the stone is going in, and stops falling the moment the stone is completely covered. Lower it further and nothing more happens.

The stone has not lost any mass or any weight. Something is pushing up on it, so the string has less to hold, and the spring stretches less. That upward push is the buoyant force.

It stops growing once the stone is covered because the stone is then displacing its own volume of water and cannot displace any more.
ch9.u6.do.steps:
1. Tie the stone to the spring balance and hang it in air. Record the reading.
2. Lower the stone until a quarter of it is under water. Record the reading.
3. Repeat with half, three quarters, and just fully covered, recording each time.
4. Now lower it another ten centimetres, well clear of the bottom, and record again.
5. Put the five readings in a table and say where the change stopped.
ch9.u6.do.watch: Make sure the stone never touches the bottom or the side of the beaker. If it does the reading drops for a completely different reason and the result looks dramatic and means nothing.
ask.ch9-u6-do-1.lost.q: Has the stone lost weight in the water?
ask.ch9-u6-do-1.lost.a:
No. Its weight is exactly what it was, because the earth has not changed and nor has the stone's mass.

What changed is how much of that weight the string has to carry. The water is now taking part of it, by pushing up, so the balance reads less. Lift the stone out and the full reading comes straight back.

The old phrase for the difference is apparent loss of weight, and the word apparent is carrying all the meaning.
a.ch9-u6-do-1.title: Weigh a stone, then lower it in
a.ch9-u6-do-1.blurb: A stone on a spring balance, lowered into water. The reading does something worth explaining.
ch9.u6.archimedes:
The experiment says there is an upward push and that it stops growing once the object is covered. Archimedes said how big it is.

When a body is immersed fully or partly in a fluid, it experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.

That is the whole principle, and it explains both halves of the experiment at once. While the stone is going in, it displaces more water with every centimetre, so the push grows. Once it is covered it is displacing its own volume and cannot displace more, so the push holds steady however deep it goes.

A floating object settles at the depth where it has displaced exactly its own weight of water. Lower it further and it displaces more than its weight, the upward push wins, and it springs back.

The principle earns its keep outside the classroom. Ships are designed with it. Submarines take water into tanks to sink and push it out to rise. A lactometer floats higher or lower in milk depending on its density, which is how watered-down milk is caught, and a hydrometer does the same for any liquid.

The story is that Archimedes noticed the water rise as he got into a bath, saw what it meant for the king's gold crown, and ran into the street shouting Eureka.
a.ch9-u6-read-2.title: Exactly how much the water pushes
ch9.u6.quiz.q0.prompt: What does Archimedes' principle say the upward force equals?
ch9.u6.quiz.q0.o0: The weight of the fluid displaced
ch9.u6.quiz.q0.f0: Right, and that is true whether the object floats or sinks.
ch9.u6.quiz.q0.f1: True only for an object that floats. A sinking object is also pushed up, by less than its weight.
ch9.u6.quiz.q0.f2: A volume is not a force. It has no newtons in it.
ch9.u6.quiz.q1.prompt: A stone is lowered deeper and deeper after it is already completely covered. What happens to the upthrust?
ch9.u6.quiz.q1.f0: Right. The stone is already displacing its own volume and cannot displace more.
ch9.u6.quiz.q1.f1: This is what the experiment is designed to disprove, and it is the commonest prediction.
ch9.u6.quiz.q1.o2: It falls away as the stone goes deeper
ch9.u6.quiz.q1.f2: Nothing about going deeper reduces the water being pushed aside.
ch9.u6.quiz.q2.prompt: You weigh 42 kg on a weighing machine in air. Is your mass more or less than 42 kg?
ch9.u6.quiz.q2.o0: More, because the air is pushing you up a little
ch9.u6.quiz.q2.f0: Right. Air is a fluid, so it gives you a small upthrust, and the machine reads a little short.
ch9.u6.quiz.q2.o1: Less, because the air is pressing you down
ch9.u6.quiz.q2.f1: The air's weight gives an upward push, not a downward one.
ch9.u6.quiz.q2.o2: Exactly 42 kg, because air has no effect
ch9.u6.quiz.q2.f2: Air is a fluid with weight, and Archimedes' principle applies to it too.
a.ch9-u6-quiz-3.title: Archimedes' principle
mis.inverse-not-inverse-square.statement: Doubling the distance halves the gravitational force.
mis.inverse-not-inverse-square.correctio: The distance is squared, so doubling it leaves a quarter of the force.
mis.force-follows-distance.statement: The gravitational force grows as the objects move apart.
mis.force-follows-distance.correction: It falls, and fast. Distance sits on the bottom of the fraction and is squared there.
mis.only-big-things-attract.statement: Only large bodies like the earth attract. Small objects do not.
mis.only-big-things-attract.correction: Every object attracts every other object. Between two small ones the force is simply too tiny to notice.
mis.bigger-mass-bigger-force.statement: The heavier of two objects pulls on the other with a larger force.
mis.bigger-mass-bigger-force.correction: The two forces are exactly equal, by the third law. What differs is the acceleration, because the masses do.
mis.earth-is-fixed.statement: The earth is fixed in space and nothing can move it.
mis.earth-is-fixed.correction: It is pulled by everything it pulls on. Its mass is so large that the acceleration is not worth measuring.
mis.heavy-falls-faster.statement: A heavier object falls faster than a light one.
mis.heavy-falls-faster.correction: It has more pull on it and exactly as much more to move. The mass cancels, and they fall together.
mis.light-falls-faster.statement: A lighter object falls faster, because there is less of it to move.
mis.light-falls-faster.correction: There is also less pull on it, by the same factor. Nothing is left over either way.
mis.light-falls-slower.statement: A sheet of paper falls slowly because it is light.
mis.light-falls-slower.correction: Crumple it and it falls fast while weighing exactly the same. What changed was the area the air could push on.
mis.paper-has-no-gravity.statement: Paper is too light to be attracted by the earth.
mis.paper-has-no-gravity.correction: Everything with mass is attracted. Air resistance is what holds a flat sheet up, and it is not a property of paper.
mis.g-is-a-speed.statement: g is a speed of 9.8 metres per second.
mis.g-is-a-speed.correction: It is an acceleration, 9.8 metres per second squared. A falling object gains 9.8 m/s in every second.
mis.g-is-a-force.statement: g is a force of 9.8 newtons.
mis.g-is-a-force.correction: It is an acceleration. The force on an object is mg, which depends on the object.
mis.g-same-everywhere.statement: g has exactly the same value everywhere on the earth.
mis.g-same-everywhere.correction: It is a little larger at the poles than at the equator, because the earth is not a perfect sphere, and it falls off with height.
mis.weight-in-kilograms.correction: Weight is a force, so it is measured in newtons. The kilogram measures mass.
mis.weight-in-pascals.correction: The pascal is the unit of pressure. Weight is a force, in newtons.
mis.mass-changes-with-place.statement: An object's mass changes when it is taken to the moon.
mis.mass-changes-with-place.correction: Mass is the amount of matter in it and does not depend on where it is. It is the weight that changes.
mis.mass-and-weight-swapped.statement: Mass changes from place to place and weight does not.
mis.mass-and-weight-swapped.correction: That is the two the wrong way round. W = mg, and it is g that varies.
mis.springs-ignore-gravity.statement: A spring balance is unaffected by gravity.
mis.springs-ignore-gravity.correction: It measures the pull on the object, which is the weight, so it reads a sixth on the moon.
mis.balances-fail-off-earth.statement: No balance works anywhere except on the earth.
mis.balances-fail-off-earth.correction: A beam balance works anywhere, because g cancels between its two pans. It is the spring balance that changes its answer.
mis.weightless-means-no-gravity.statemen: Astronauts float because there is no gravity in orbit.
mis.weightless-means-no-gravity.correcti: The earth's pull there is still about nine tenths of what it is on the ground. They float because the station and everything in it are falling together.
mis.pressure-is-force-times-area.stateme: Pressure is force multiplied by area.
mis.pressure-is-force-times-area.correct: It is force divided by area, which is why a sharp tip presses harder than a flat head under the same push.
mis.pressure-is-weight.statement: Pressure and weight are the same thing.
mis.pressure-is-weight.correction: The weight supplies the thrust. The pressure also depends on how much area that thrust is spread over.
mis.thin-strap-is-heavier.statement: A thin bag strap makes the bag heavier.
mis.thin-strap-is-heavier.correction: The bag's weight is unchanged. The strap concentrates it onto less of your shoulder, which raises the pressure.
mis.thin-strap-pulls-harder.statement: A thin strap pulls down with a larger force than a broad one.
mis.thin-strap-pulls-harder.correction: The pull is the weight of the bag either way. Only the area taking it is different.
mis.thrust-changes-with-face.statement: Turning a block onto a different face changes the thrust it exerts.
mis.thrust-changes-with-face.correction: The thrust is the block's weight, which is the same whichever way up it is. The area changes, so the pressure does.
mis.lighter-things-float.statement: Lighter objects float and heavier ones sink.
mis.lighter-things-float.correction: A ship weighs thousands of tonnes and floats. It is density that decides, not mass.
mis.smaller-things-float.statement: Small objects float and large ones sink.
mis.smaller-things-float.correction: A pin is tiny and sinks. Size does not enter into it.
mis.upthrust-acts-down.statement: The buoyant force acts downwards on an immersed object.
mis.upthrust-acts-down.correction: It acts vertically upwards, which is why it opposes the weight and makes things feel lighter in water.
mis.upthrust-follows-motion.statement: The buoyant force points whichever way the object is moving.
mis.upthrust-follows-motion.correction: It is upwards whether the object is rising, sinking or still.
mis.water-has-no-weight.statement: Water has no weight of its own.
mis.water-has-no-weight.correction: It is heavy, and its weight is exactly where the upthrust comes from.
mis.no-gravity-under-water.statement: Gravity does not act on objects under water.
mis.no-gravity-under-water.correction: It acts everywhere. An object under water has its full weight, and the upthrust works against it.
mis.upthrust-equals-object-weight.statem: The upthrust always equals the weight of the object.
mis.upthrust-equals-object-weight.correc: Only for something that floats. The principle says it equals the weight of the fluid displaced, and for a sinking object that is less.
mis.upthrust-is-a-volume.statement: The upthrust equals the volume of fluid displaced.
mis.upthrust-is-a-volume.correction: A volume is not a force. It is the weight of that volume of fluid.
mis.upthrust-grows-with-depth.statement: The deeper a submerged object goes, the larger the upthrust on it.
mis.upthrust-grows-with-depth.correction: Once it is fully covered it displaces its own volume and can displace no more, so the upthrust holds steady.
mis.upthrust-falls-with-depth.statement: The upthrust gets weaker the deeper an object goes.
mis.upthrust-falls-with-depth.correction: It is unchanged once the object is fully covered. Nothing about depth reduces the water pushed aside.
mis.air-presses-down.statement: Air presses an object downwards, so a weighing machine over-reads.
mis.air-presses-down.correction: Air is a fluid and gives a small upthrust, so a weighing machine reads very slightly short.
mis.air-has-no-upthrust.statement: Archimedes' principle applies only to liquids.
mis.air-has-no-upthrust.correction: It applies to all fluids, and air is one. The effect is small because air is not very dense.
recap.s.u1.q1.ask: State the universal law of gravitation.
recap.s.u1.q1.answer: Every object in the universe attracts every other object with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres. F = G Mm over d squared.
recap.s.u1.q1.listenFor: Listen for the square being dropped, so that doubling the distance halves the force instead of quartering it. That one word is the law.
recap.s.u1.q2.ask: The distance between two objects is tripled. Tell me what happens to the force, and by how much.
recap.s.u1.q2.answer: It falls to a ninth of what it was, because three squared is nine and the distance is squared on the bottom.
recap.s.u1.q2.listenFor: Listen for a third. It is the answer you get by forgetting the square, and it sounds reasonable, which is why it survives.
recap.s.u2.q1.ask: A 1 kg stone and a 10 kg stone are dropped together with no air in the way. Explain which lands first.
recap.s.u2.q1.answer: Neither. They land together. The earth pulls ten times as hard on the heavier one, and it has ten times as much mass to move, so a = F/m comes out the same for both.
recap.s.u2.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'the heavy one, because gravity pulls it harder'. The first half of that is true, and the answer still comes out wrong, which makes it worth working through rather than correcting.
recap.s.u2.q2.ask: Why does a flat sheet of paper fall more slowly than the same sheet crumpled into a ball?
recap.s.u2.q2.answer: Air resistance. The flat sheet gives the air a large area to push against. Crumpling changes the area and nothing else, and the mass is identical.
recap.s.u2.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'the ball is heavier'. Weighing the two settles it in five seconds and is worth doing.
recap.s.u3.q1.ask: Name the unit of mass and the unit of weight, and say which one changes on the moon.
recap.s.u3.q1.answer: Mass is in kilograms, weight is in newtons. The weight changes, to about a sixth, because g on the moon is about a sixth of g here. The mass does not change at all.
recap.s.u3.q1.listenFor: Listen for weight given in kilograms. It is what every shop sign says, and it is the root of most of the confusion in this topic.
recap.s.u3.q2.ask: A beam balance and a spring balance are taken to the moon. Explain which still gives the right answer.
recap.s.u3.q2.answer: The beam balance. It compares the pull on the unknown with the pull on known weights in the same gravity, so g cancels. The spring balance measures the pull itself and reads a sixth.
recap.s.u3.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'neither works on the moon'. Both still work. Only one of them still means what it meant here.
recap.s.u4.q1.ask: Give the relationship between thrust, pressure and area.
recap.s.u4.q1.answer: Pressure is thrust divided by area, in newtons per square metre, which is the pascal.
recap.s.u4.q1.listenFor: Listen for thrust multiplied by area. That would make a broad foot press harder than a sharp pin, which is the opposite of every example in the topic.
recap.s.u4.q2.ask: A block is turned from a small face onto a large one. Tell me what changes and what does not.
recap.s.u4.q2.answer: The thrust does not change: it is the weight of the block, and turning it over does not alter that. The area goes up, so the pressure comes down.
recap.s.u4.q2.listenFor: Listen for the thrust being said to fall as well. It is a useful check in any problem of this kind.
recap.s.u5.q1.ask: What decides whether an object floats or sinks in water?
recap.s.u5.q1.answer: Its density compared with the density of the water. Less dense floats, more dense sinks. Mass and size on their own decide nothing.
recap.s.u5.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'whether it is heavy'. A ship is thousands of tonnes and floats, and a pin is a few grams and sinks.
recap.s.u5.q2.ask: You push a sealed empty bottle further and further into water. Describe what the upward push does.
recap.s.u5.q2.answer: It grows while more of the bottle is going under, and stops growing the moment the bottle is completely covered. Deeper than that, nothing changes.
recap.s.u5.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'it keeps growing all the way down'. It is the natural guess and it is what the activity is built to test.
recap.s.u6.q1.answer: When a body is immersed fully or partly in a fluid, it experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.
recap.s.u6.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'equal to the weight of the object'. That is true only when the object floats, and a stone on a spring balance shows it failing.
recap.s.u6.q2.ask: A stone on a spring balance reads less once it is in water. Explain what has happened to its weight.
recap.s.u6.q2.answer: Nothing. The weight is exactly what it was. The water is now carrying part of it by pushing up, so the string has less to hold and the spring stretches less.
recap.s.u6.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'it lost weight in the water'. The old name for it is apparent loss of weight, and the word apparent is where the whole answer lives.
aid.s.u3.meaning: Five tests that separate mass from weight, and the word names the place where they come apart. Carry a 10 kg bag to the moon and it is still 10 kg of bag, and it weighs a sixth of what it did.
aid.s.u3.L.property: Location: does it change when you move?
aid.s.u3.L.a: Never. The same number on the earth, on the moon and in deep space.
aid.s.u3.L.b: Yes. It follows g, and g follows where you happen to be.
aid.s.u3.U.property: Unit: what is it measured in?
aid.s.u3.U.b: Newtons, because it is a force.
aid.s.u3.N.property: Nil: can it ever come out as zero?
aid.s.u3.N.a: Never, for anything made of matter at all.
aid.s.u3.N.b: Very nearly, far enough from any planet.
aid.s.u3.A.property: Arrow: does it have a direction?
aid.s.u3.A.a: No. It is a plain amount with nowhere to point.
aid.s.u3.A.b: Yes, straight down, towards the centre of the earth.
aid.s.u3.R.a: A beam balance, which compares two pans standing in the same gravity.
aid.s.u3.R.b: A spring balance, which measures the pull on the object itself.
gloss.gravitation: The attraction between any two objects that have mass. It acts everywhere in the universe, never cancels, and never pushes.
gloss.universal-law: The force between two objects is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres.
gloss.universal-law.forms: universal law of gravitation|universal law|law of gravitation
gloss.gravitational-constant: G, the constant in the universal law, equal to 6.673 times ten to the minus eleven N m squared per kg squared. Measured by Henry Cavendish.
gloss.centripetal-force: The force that keeps a body moving on a circular path, directed towards the centre. For the moon it is supplied by the earth's gravitation.
gloss.tangent: A straight line that meets a circle at exactly one point. A body released from a circular path travels along it.
gloss.free-fall: Motion in which gravitation is the only force acting. Every object in free fall has the same acceleration, whatever its mass.
gloss.acceleration-due-to-gravity: g, the acceleration of a freely falling object, about 9.8 metres per second squared at the earth's surface. It comes from g = GM over R squared.
gloss.acceleration-due-to-gravity.forms: acceleration due to gravity|g|acceleration due to gravitational force
gloss.mass: The amount of matter in an object, and the measure of its inertia. Measured in kilograms, and the same wherever the object is taken.
gloss.weight: The force with which the earth attracts an object, equal to mg. Measured in newtons, directed downwards, and different on the moon.
gloss.thrust: The force acting on a surface at right angles to it. For an object resting on a table, it is the object's weight.
gloss.pressure: Thrust per unit area. The same force gives a large pressure on a small area and a small pressure on a large one.
gloss.pascal: The SI unit of pressure, equal to one newton per square metre. Named after Blaise Pascal.
gloss.buoyancy: The upward force a fluid exerts on anything immersed in it. Also called upthrust, and it is what makes an object feel lighter in water.
gloss.density: Mass per unit volume. An object less dense than a liquid floats on it, and one more dense sinks.
gloss.archimedes-principle: A body immersed fully or partly in a fluid experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces.
